chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Ali, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Sa'd ibn al-Jallab, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, Allah (Exalted and Majestic) did not make al-ghayrah (sense of honor/jealousy) for the women, and rather it is the evil ones of them who express it; as for the believing women, they do not. But rather, Allah made al-ghayrah for the men because He permitted the man four (wives) and whatever his right hand possesses, and did not make it for the woman except for her husband. So if she were to intend someone else along with him, she would be an adulteress in the Presence of Allah.

He said, and Al-Qasim ibn Yahya reported it from his grandfather Al-Hasan ibn Rashid, from Abu Bakr al-Hadrami, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), except that he said: 'So if she were to be immoral with someone else along with him'.

key_terms.الْغَيْرَةُ: Sense of honor, jealousy, or protective zeal
key_terms.مَا مَلَكَتْ يَمِينُهُ: What his right hand possesses (concubines/slave girls)

ai.seo_question: Why is the sense of honor (al-ghayrah) designated for men rather than women in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In Shia scholarship, this hadith distinguishes between 'ghayrah' (protective jealousy/honor) and 'ghirah' (possessive jealousy), asserting that the former is a masculine trait aligned with the asymmetry of marital rights (polygyny for men, monogamy for women). The variant reading 'baghat' (committed fornication) in the chain of Qasim ibn Yahya emphasizes the legal consequence of a woman seeking extra-marital relations, reinforcing the theological link between gender-specific rights and spiritual accountability.
